hints: A queue naturally visits nodes in top-to-bottom, left-to-right order. The tricky part is knowing where one row ends and the next begins.
Use level-order BFS. Before processing a row, store size = q.size(): exactly that many nodes form the current row, and the children you push belong to the next row.

1. If root is null return an empty list.
  2. Push root into a queue.
  3. While the queue is not empty: size = q.size(), make an empty row.
  4. Pop size nodes, add each value to the row, push left then right child.
  5. Add the row to the answer.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For each depth from 0 to the height, run a DFS that collects the nodes at exactly that depth, left to right.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: One BFS that groups nodes by row using the queue size at the start of each level (a DFS that passes depth and appends to rows[depth] also works).

explain: For [8,3,11,null,6,9]: 8 has children 3 and 11; 3 has only a right child 6; 11 has a left child 9. Row 0 is [8]. With size 2, row 1 pops 3 and 11 and pushes 6 then 9. Row 2 is [6,9], so the answer is [[8],[3,11],[6,9]]. Pushing left before right keeps each row in left-to-right order. Edge case: an empty tree returns [].
recognize: 'Group values by depth, left to right' → BFS with a queue, one loop iteration per level.
